name: Single-Leg Stand
summary: Standing on one leg with a support within reach. Simple and easy to measure, it practices the ankle and hip control that keeps you steady on your feet.
steps: Stand tall beside a kitchen counter or sturdy chair, feet hip-width apart, with one hand resting lightly on the support.
Shift your weight onto one foot, keeping that knee soft and not locked.
Lift the other foot a few centimeters off the floor and hold your hips level.
Fix your eyes on a point ahead of you and breathe normally. Aim to hold for 10 to 30 seconds.
Lower the foot with control, then repeat on the other leg. Do two or three holds per side.
cues: Stand tall, as if growing upward
Soft knee on the standing leg
Fingertips on the support, not a tight grip
mistakes: Hiking or dropping one hip
Locking the standing knee
Looking down at your feet
Practicing far from any support when your balance is shaky
easier: Keep both hands on the support, or rest the toes of the lifted foot lightly on the floor.
harder: Take your hand off the support, turn your head slowly from side to side, or stand on a folded towel.

name: Tandem Walk
summary: Walking heel to toe along a straight line, as if on a tightrope. It narrows your base of support and trains the balance you need on uneven ground.
steps: Stand tall next to a wall or along a kitchen counter, with a clear path of about three to five meters (10 to 16 feet) ahead of you.
Place one foot directly in front of the other so the heel of the front foot touches, or nearly touches, the toes of the back foot.
Look ahead, not at your feet, and shift your weight onto the front foot.
Bring the back foot forward and place it heel to toe in front, moving slowly and with control.
Take 10 to 20 steps, turn around carefully and walk back. Repeat two or three times.
cues: Tall posture, arms out if needed
mistakes: Looking down at your feet the whole time
Rushing to avoid the wobble
Stepping wide of the line
Practicing without a wall or counter in reach when your balance is unsteady
easier: Keep a hand on the wall or counter, or leave a small gap between heel and toe.
harder: Walk without support, turn your head slowly as you walk, or try it backward beside a counter.

name: Single-Leg Romanian Deadlift Reach
summary: A one-legged hip hinge with no weight, reaching your hands toward the floor. It blends balance with hip strength and teaches control you can later load.
steps: Stand tall on your left leg with the knee slightly bent, next to a wall or chair you can touch if needed.
Brace your midsection and keep your hips square to the front.
Hinge forward at the hips, reaching both hands toward the floor in front of you while your right leg extends straight back behind you.
Lower until your torso and back leg form a line close to parallel with the floor, or as far as you can go with a flat back and steady balance.
Squeeze the glute of your standing leg to return to tall standing. Do 6 to 10 reps, then switch legs.
cues: Torso and back leg move as one seesaw
Reach long through the back heel
mistakes: Opening the hip of the raised leg out to the side
Rounding the back to reach the floor
Locking the standing knee
Rushing down and losing balance at the bottom
easier: Slide one hand along a wall or chair back, or keep the toes of the back foot on the floor for support.
harder: Hold a light dumbbell in the hand opposite the standing leg, or pause for two seconds at the bottom.

name: Heel-to-Toe Raise
summary: Rising onto your toes, then rocking back onto your heels, with a support in reach. It strengthens the calf and shin muscles and practices shifting your weight under control.
steps: Stand tall behind a sturdy chair or at a counter, feet hip-width apart, with both hands resting lightly on the support.
Rise slowly onto the balls of your feet, lifting your heels as high as is comfortable.
Pause for a second, then lower your heels back to the floor with control.
Now rock your weight back onto your heels and lift your toes and the front of your feet off the floor. Keep your hips over your ankles; do not stick them out behind you.
Pause, lower your toes and continue alternating heel raises and toe raises for 10 to 15 slow rounds.
mistakes: Bending at the hips and sticking the backside out during the toe raise
Rocking quickly with momentum
Leaning heavily on the support
Letting the ankles roll outward on the heel raise
easier: Do the heel raises and toe raises as separate sets, or do them seated with your feet flat on the floor.
harder: Use only your fingertips on the support, then no hands, or hold each end position for three seconds.

name: Sit-to-Stand
summary: Standing up from a chair and sitting back down without using your hands. It builds the leg strength and control behind one of the most important movements of daily life.
steps: Sit toward the front of a sturdy chair that cannot slide, ideally one placed against a wall. Put your feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart and slightly behind your knees.
Cross your arms over your chest, or reach them forward for balance.
Lean your chest forward over your thighs, nose over toes, and press through your whole feet to stand up fully.
Stand tall for a moment with hips and knees straight.
Reach your hips back and lower yourself slowly, taking about three seconds to touch the seat. Do not drop into it.
Repeat for 8 to 12 reps, resting as needed.
cues: Knees stay in line with the toes
Sit down as if the chair were fragile
mistakes: Dropping onto the seat instead of lowering with control
Rocking back and forth to build momentum
Letting the knees fall inward
Using a chair that slides or has wheels
easier: Push off the armrests or your thighs with your hands, or raise the seat with a firm cushion.
harder: Use a lower seat, hover just above the chair for two seconds before sitting, or hold a weight at your chest.

name: Clock Reach
summary: Balancing on one leg while the other foot taps points around an imaginary clock face. It challenges your balance in several directions, the way real life does.
steps: Stand on your left leg in the center of an imaginary clock face, next to a chair or counter you can touch. Bend the standing knee slightly.
Reach your right foot forward and lightly tap the floor at 12 o'clock without putting weight on it, then bring it back to the center.
Tap out to the side at 3 o'clock, then behind you at 6 o'clock, returning to the center each time.
Keep your hips level, your chest tall and your standing knee pointing over your toes on every reach.
Complete three to five trips around the clock. Then stand on your right leg and tap 12, 9 and 6 o'clock with your left foot.
cues: Tap lightly, as if testing thin ice
Reach only as far as you can control
mistakes: Shifting your weight onto the tapping foot
Letting the standing knee collapse inward
Leaning the trunk far over to reach further
Speeding up and losing control
easier: Hold the support, keep the reaches short and rest the tapping foot on the floor between taps.
harder: Reach further and bend the standing knee more, add taps at the diagonal points, or let go of the support.
